placementGuide.ability: Greet people and order food, not much more
Chat in the present tense but stall on anything in the past
Tell a simple story in the past (with errors) and follow slow Spanish
Hold your own with a teacher but get lost at the family table

phases.title: Foundations
phases.goal: By week 8 you can manage a five-minute conversation about yourself, your family and last weekend without falling back on English.
habits: Main course for this phase: one audio-first beginner course, worked through in order.
Start the tutor in week 1, not week 8; early sessions can be mostly scripted.
phases.exitCheck: Five minutes with your tutor on yourself, your family and last weekend, no English.

blocks.grammar: Sounds and spelling; ser vs estar; gender and articles; regular present tense
blocks.familyTask: Greet and say goodbye in Spanish every single time; ask ¿Cómo están? and understand the answer

blocks.grammar: Irregular present (tener, ir, querer, poder, hacer); gustar; question words
blocks.vocabulary: Food and drink, the house, days and times
blocks.familyTask: Ask what they are cooking, offer a drink, say what you like

blocks.grammar: Preterite: regular verbs plus fui, hice, tuve, estuve; ir a + infinitive for the future
blocks.familyTask: Tell them one thing you did this week and one thing you will do next week

blocks.grammar: Imperfect basics; object pronouns (lo, la, le); reflexive verbs
blocks.familyTask: Ask one question about their life in Chile and follow up once

phases.title: Conversation core
phases.goal: By week 20 you can hold a 20-minute conversation and tell a three-minute story in the past.
habits: Weekly diary: 150 words on your week, corrected by your tutor.
Shadowing: 5 minutes a day repeating a native speaker's audio out loud, half a second behind them.
One Chilean episode a week: a slow Chilean podcast for learners, so the accent is familiar before Phase 3.
phases.exitCheck: 20 minutes of conversation with your tutor; a three-minute past-tense story; a slow learner podcast understood without a transcript.

blocks.grammar: Preterite vs imperfect in storytelling; connectors (entonces, pero, porque, aunque, o sea)
blocks.conversationFocus: Anecdotes: how you met your wife, a trip, a bad day
blocks.familyTask: Tell one prepared two-minute story; ask them for one back

blocks.grammar: Present perfect; commands (páseme, siéntese, pruebe); comparisons
blocks.familyTask: Cook one dish together with instructions in Spanish only

blocks.grammar: Present subjunctive after quiero que, espero que, ojalá, cuando
blocks.conversationFocus: Opinions, hopes, plans for the family
blocks.familyTask: Go through an old photo album; they narrate, you ask questions

blocks.grammar: Conditional and future; por vs para; impersonal se
blocks.conversationFocus: Hypotheticals, travel, what Chile is like
blocks.familyTask: Swap two voice notes a week on WhatsApp

phases.title: The Chilean ear
phases.goal: By week 32 you can follow the thread of a dinner-table conversation between Chileans and rejoin it after losing your place.
habits: Move your daily listening to Chilean sources: start with podcasts made for learners, step up to 31 Minutos, then to native podcasts, radio and TV news.
Transcribe one minute of Chilean audio. Write what you hear, then check it with your tutor; the gaps show exactly which sounds you are missing.
Drill one sound change from the cheat sheet until you can both hear it and produce it.
Collect 10 chilenismos, taking them from your in-laws first and from podcasts second.
Ask your tutor for natural speed in the last 10 minutes of every session.
phases.grammarNote: Grammar still to cover, one topic per fortnight: imperfect subjunctive, si clauses (si tuviera…, iría), reported speech, relative clauses, and recognising the Chilean voseo forms.
phases.exitCheck: Summarise a 10-minute native Chilean podcast segment to your tutor; get through the Spanish-only meal.

blocks.familyTask: Ask them to teach you one Chilean word or saying per visit, with an example
Watch a Chilean programme or match together and talk about it afterwards
First Spanish-only meal; agree beforehand that nobody rescues you in English

phases.title: Family fluency
phases.goal: By week 52 you can spend an hour in Spanish with your in-laws on almost any everyday topic, including humour and disagreement.
habits: Structured study shrinks to one session a week, driven by the error log your tutor keeps.
Spanish-only meals: fortnightly from week 33, weekly from week 41.
Family history interviews: one 20-minute conversation a month about their lives in Chile; record it with their permission and re-listen for words you missed.
Phone and voice notes: audio with no faces or gestures is the hardest test, so make it routine.
Reading: short Chilean news articles weekly; later a short contemporary Chilean novel or story collection, a few pages a day.
Topics to stretch into: Chilean food and regions, football, politics and history (listen more than you talk), family jokes and sayings.
phases.exitCheck: An hour of unscripted conversation with your in-laws in which nobody switches to English.

capstone.label: Give a two-minute toast in Spanish at a family occasion.
capstone.note: Fiestas Patrias on 18 September 2027 lands at about week 44 and suits it well.

weeklySlots.label: Vocabulary review
weeklySlots.purpose: Spaced-repetition flashcards; about 10 new cards a day, drawn from that week's theme and from words your in-laws actually use

weeklySlots.label: Listening
weeklySlots.purpose: Audio at your level – commute, dog walk, dishes

weeklySlots.label: Structured study
weeklySlots.purpose: The grammar point of the week, then 5 sentences of your own using it

weeklySlots.label: Tutor conversation
weeklySlots.purpose: A Chilean tutor; half free conversation, half correction of your mistakes

weeklySlots.label: Family task
weeklySlots.purpose: The task listed for that week, done with your in-laws in person or by voice note

sounds.pattern: s at the end of a syllable turns into a breath or vanishes
ch can soften towards sh for some speakers

cheatSheet.voseoNote: In casual speech the tú forms change their endings. It is spoken, informal and never written in formal contexts. Understand it early; use it with peers once it feels natural.
cheatSheet.ustedNote: Many Chilean families use usted with parents-in-law as a sign of respect, others use tú. Start with usted and ask them which they prefer; the family tasks in this plan use the usted/ustedes forms.

words.meaning: Late-afternoon tea with bread, often replacing dinner
Mate, or idiot, depending on tone; everywhere in casual speech
words.example: Recognise it; do not aim it at your suegros.

cheatSheet.diminutivesNote: Diminutives are constant and affectionate: un tecito, un ratito, al tirito.

jobs: Tell them the goal and the date — say you want to hold a full conversation with them in Spanish by November 2027.
Ask for three things: speak a little slower rather than switching to English; correct one mistake per conversation, not every one; teach you one word each visit.
Settle usted or tú in the first week.
Bring one prepared question to every visit. Preparation lowers the nerves, and their answer is free listening practice.
questions: ¿Cómo era su barrio cuando eran chicos?
¿Qué se comía en su casa los domingos?
¿Qué es lo que más echan de menos de Chile?
¿Qué palabra chilena debería aprender esta semana?
family.cookingNote: Cooking together works at every level because the vocabulary is concrete and repeated.
